articles.title: Watch: Shipwreck found on Nantucket island during nor'easter storm
articles.summary: The so-called nor'easter storm has washed up what may be a shipwreck from the 19th century in Massachusetts, local media says.
articles.body:
A powerful nor'easter storm has washed up what may be a shipwreck from the 19th century in Massachusetts, local media said.

The wreckage discovered on a beach on Sunday is believed to be part of the "Warren Sawyer" – which ran aground near Nantucket in 1884, according to the Nantucket Current.

articles.title: The Supreme Court just threw a new monkey wrench at the midterms. Here’s what to know
articles.summary: Election Day is fast approaching, but the Supreme Court is still weighing in on the rules, most recently on Friday when it allowed states to use a Trump admi...
articles.body:
A version of this story appeared in CNN's What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .

Election Day is fast approaching, but the Supreme Court is still weighing in on the rules — most recently on Friday when it allowed states to use a Trump administration - backed tool to ferret out noncitizen voting there's little evidence occurs in a widespread way.

Nobody wants noncitizens voting illegally, but the move by justices less than two months from Election Day raises the real concern that legal citizen voters could find themselves unable to cast ballots.

Supreme Court justices have already been faced with multiple questions about the coming election.

They gutted the Voting Rights Act , supercharging a race to redraw congressional maps this year and into the future.

One state, Missouri , was still wondering Friday which congressional districts its voters would cast ballots in come November because lower courts weighed in after the high court. Never mind that ballots had already been printed and mailed.

An unsigned Friday evening decision from the Supreme Court — which sided with opponents of the proposed districts for the third time in as many weeks — seemed likely to put to rest a whirlwind legal saga that bounced through state and federal courts for much of September. Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe said Friday that Missouri would follow the court's order.

While the justices in other cases blessed the redrawing of maps for partisan gain, they hit pause, at least for now, on the Trump administration's plan to upend mail-in voting writ large, tabling that issue for the next election.

Noncitizen voting has been a bugbear for Trump for years. He has alleged there is widespread fraud even in elections he won, although neither of his administrations has been able to find much evidence.

I asked CNN's Fredreka Schouten, a national political writer, about the database this decision unleashes and what it could mean for people trying to cast ballots.

SCHOUTEN: It's a federal tool known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements. It's been around for decades and has long been used to verify the citizenship and immigration status of people seeking government benefits. And some election officials have had agreements in the past to use the tool, for a fee, to check the citizenship status of voters.

But the Trump administration dramatically revamped it, starting last year. It's now linked to lots of government data as part of the administration's push to hunt for potential noncitizens on the voting rolls.

Does it have anything to do with the SAVE America Act that Trump tried, unsuccessfully, to pass?

SCHOUTEN: The SAVE America Act is different but sort of related in that they are both focused on the question of whether only US citizens are casting ballots.

The SAVE America Act would have dramatically revamped voting rules across the country, requiring voter ID to cast a ballot and mandating that people provide documents, such as a birth certificate of US passport, proving their citizenship when they register to vote. It would also put pressure on states to use the SAVE data system and other data tools like it for purging rolls.

Critics say many legitimate voters don't have easy access to those documents and argue the proposal would have disenfranchised many Americans.

I should say here that experts note that voting by noncitizens in federal elections, which is already illegal, is exceedingly rare. But this has become an animating issue for the president.

SCHOUTEN: The Trump administration linked the information already in SAVE to other federal data, most notably Social Security Administration records, which cover most Americans.

The administration then encouraged election officials to carry out bulk uploads of their states' registration rolls and waived any fee to do so. Tens of millions of records were run through the system before a federal judge blocked its use earlier this year.

With Friday's ruling, the US Supreme Court has allowed SAVE to be used again for reviewing voter rolls.

What does this mean for the midterms, now just weeks away?

The high court's opinion emphasized that SAVE can be used for "individualized" checks of a voter's citizenship in the upcoming election but also noted that federal law prohibits mass purges close to Election Day.

But the administration has argued that the federal ban on mass removals within 90 days of an election doesn't apply to purges involving noncitizens who were improperly registered in the first place. The Supreme Court will decide that question in a case this coming term — but not before the midterms.

States — including red states — have refused to give the federal government their voter rolls. How did the administration get around that?

In addition to encouraging states to use SAVE to conduct their own reviews of their voting rolls, the Justice Department has been on a campaign to obtain each state's full, unredacted lists of voters, including personal information about voters, such as full dates or birth and partial Social Security numbers, to do its own check on whether states are complying with federal law.

When those states refused, the DOJ sued. So far, the agency has lost all 25 cases in which a judge has ruled.

But federal agencies have moved forward with efforts to try to find potential noncitizens on voting rolls — including using publicly available voter lists. A recent whistleblower complaint released by several Democrats on Capitol Hill alleged that agents in the Department of Homeland Security, who were tasked with rooting out voter fraud, are being kept in the dark about the sources of some of the data being used in their reviews.

And the dispute the Supreme Court was ruling on Friday was the administration's ability to offer the SAVE systems to states that want to voluntarily want to use it for their own voter list maintenance.

SCHOUTEN: One overarching worry from critics of the SAVE tool is that it's not reliable.

Take Texas, for example. State officials there ran all 18 million names of its voters through the SAVE tool last year and announced that their audit had found 2,724 potential noncitizens and directed counties to give voters 30 days to verify their citizenship or be removed from the rolls.

Those numbers began dropping once local election officials began digging — in part, because the system doesn't appear to properly track naturalized citizens.

Earlier this year, I interviewed a Texas resident who became ensnared by the audit. She was born in Argentina and was a naturalized US citizen, yet state officials tagged her as a suspected noncitizen. She was able to quickly send in a scan of her US passport and remain a voter.

Earlier this month, Texas officials announced that hundreds of potential noncitizens flagged last year were indeed Americans and eligible to vote and called on local officials to reinstate their registrations if they had been removed.

Say I'm a citizen who loses their registration because of a mistake. How will I know before Election Day? What can I do?

SCHOUTEN: If you are worried about this or any other voting issue, you can always verify your registration status with your local election office. There's enough time before the general election to fix any problems.

CNN's Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title: Economist calls out America’s socialist elite, says they got rich bashing capitalism
articles.summary: Stephen Moore says Bernie Sanders, Hasan Piker and Elizabeth Warren grew wealthy under capitalism while pushing socialist policies they call immoral.
articles.body:
Economist Stephen Moore highlights how prominent socialist figures in the US, such as Bernie Sanders and Hasan Piker, have amassed wealth within the capitalist system they criticize.

Moore questions the hypocrisy of wealthy socialist advocates who benefit from capitalism while advocating for wealth redistribution policies, suggesting they should lead by example and give more to the poor.

The economist emphasizes that the US uniquely rewards individuals who critique free-market capitalism, attracting people from socialist countries who have witnessed the failures of socialism in their own nations.

Socialist and progressive figures have found a lucrative platform attacking capitalism, according to economist Stephen Moore, who says they have grown wealthy inside the free-market system they want to overhaul.

Moore, a former senior economic advisor to President Trump, told Fox News Digital in an interview that the United States is uniquely positioned to reward people who criticize capitalism.

He said public figures, including Sen. Bernie Sanders and online political commentator Hasan Piker, have benefited from the wealth and opportunities created by the American economy while advocating socialist policies.

"There's no country in the world where you can get rich off of attacking free-market capitalism better than in the United States," Moore told Fox Digital. "And, so, you have dozens of these prominent voices in the socialist movement on the Democratic side who actually are rich, millionaires or more, and they attack the very system that made them rich in the first place."

Moore said a recent USA Today opinion piece made a similar argument. The story was titled, "Hasan Piker's luxury lifestyle isn't what Marx had in mind."

It read in part, "America's loudest democratic socialists have a problem: Many of them are too rich. Hasan Piker; Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.; Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass; and an entire class of young socialist influencers are all wealthy. Yet even though their wealth was acquired through a capitalist system they see as immoral, they give very little of it away."

"It is remarkable how many of these leading, so-called advocates of socialism have come from rich families or have gotten rich on capitalism themselves," Moore said. "So, even people like Bernie Sanders are wondering whether there's a degree of hypocrisy here. I mean, there's a reason why just about everybody in the world wants to come to the United States. It's not because we have socialism. It's because we have free-market capitalism."

Moore also questioned whether wealthy advocates of wealth redistribution should voluntarily give up more of their own assets and challenged progressive leaders to explain why they continue to benefit from capitalism while criticizing it.

"I think the capital H is for hypocrisy here, and if these people really believed and share the wealth policies that they keep espousing, maybe they could start with themselves," Moore said.

"Maybe they could sell some of these assets and give the money to the poor, but it turns out, by the way, that liberal socialists tend to be the least generous in terms of charitable giving. There was a very famous book on this. So, it turns out that free-market capitalists tend to be very generous in sharing their wealth, but not so much so democratic socialists."

The economist said some socialists try to conceal their wealth to appeal more to the public.

"They try to hide their wealth from Americans so they can pretend like they are working-class people," Moore said. "But if you look at the people who are really at the head of the democratic socialist movement and the people who are spending a lot of money, those tend to be very rich people themselves.

"This is, as I said before, this is the only country where you can get rich off of attacking the free-market capitalism system, which really creates the wealth in the United States in the first place. It's the reason why so many people come to this country from socialist countries, and they get here, and they say they don't understand why anyone would want to have more socialism in America when they've seen it fail in their own country."

Fox News Digital reached out to Piker , Sanders and Warren for comment.

articles.title: Lula sugere conselho para indicar ministros do STF e defende filho | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente também defendeu Lulinha e Marcola em investigações da PF sobre suposto tráfico de influência e corrupção envolvendo o Ministério da Saúde e o MDS.
articles.summary: Lula propõe conselho para indicações ao STF e defende a inocência de seu filho, Lulinha, em investigações da PF sobre suposto tráfico de influência no governo.
articles.body:
Lula em entrevista à Band neste domingo (27). — Foto: Reprodução

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva afirmou neste domingo (27), que não quer mais deixar as indicações para ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) na decisão do presidente e que sugeriu criar um conselho para avaliar as indicações.

"A única coisa que eu posso dizer é que não pode continuar do jeito que está", criticou o presidente.

"Eu quero mudar o critério de escolha, porque o critério de escolha é muito vulnerável. Acho que nós temos que criar um critério para envolver a sociedade civil para que a gente indicar alguém que não seja da vontade do presidente. Tem que ser alguém que seja que passe por um crivo de um colegiado que a gente vai ter que pensar como criar para aquela pessoa não seja um cara indicado pelo presidente", afirmou.

A declaração foi dada durante entrevista à TV Bandeirantes, gravada no Palácio da Alvorada nesta manhã.

Lula ainda afirmou que é as indicações precisam analisar "com muito mais cuidado a biografia das pessoas que vão assumir a Suprema Corte", para que elas tenham uma linha de coerência e responsabilidade durante sua atuação.

"Eu estou preocupado agora é com o critério de indicação. Estou preocupado com o mandato, O cidadão não pode ser 40 anos 45 anos 35 anos", disse.

O presidente ainda ironizou que os ministros da Suprema Corte, após serem indicados, acreditam que viram deuses.

"Uma coisa é quando você indica, outra coisa é quando bota toga. E quando o cara coloca a toga, ele vira Deus", reclamou.

Durante a entrevista, Lula continuou criticando os ministros ao dizer que os integrantes precisam "ter mamuita seriedade" e que eles não deveriam assumir com a pretenção de ficar ricos.

"Um ministro não pode querer ficar rico, é incompatível a função de quem recebe R$ 43 mil e ficar rico, não é compatível. Da mesma forma que o deputado. Nenhum salário de deputado, de governador, de presidente, pode deixar alguém rico", afirmou.

Marcola, ex-chefe de gabinete do presidente Lula, Roberta Luchsinger e Fábio Luis Lula da Silva, o Lulinha — Foto: Reprodução

O presidente também falou que acredita na inocência do seu filho, Fábio Luis, conhecido como Lulinha, investigado pela relação que tem com a lobbysta Roberta Luchsinger. O presidente também saiu em defesa do seu ex-chefe de gabinete, Marco Aurélio Santana Ribeiro, o Marcola.

Uma das linhas de investigação apura se Lulinha atuou para favorecer o lobista Antônio Carlos Camilo Antunes, conhecido como "Careca do INSS", em negociações com o Ministério da Saúde.

O "Careca do INSS" é apontado como um dos principais responsáveis pelos desvios de aposentadorias e pensões.

A PF também identificou que o ex-chefe de gabinete de Lula, Marco Aurélio Santana, o Marcola, recebeu a minuta do contrato para a venda de medicamentos à base de canabidiol ao Ministério da Saúde.

As mensagens analisadas pela PF mostram que a empresária Roberta Luchsinger mantinha malas com grande quantidade de dinheiro vivo para fazer pagamentos. Em março de 2023, em uma conversa, Ulisses Barbosa, auxiliar pessoal e motorista de Roberta disse:

"Trouxe a mala. Um lado tá os 500k - 500 mil. Dou o outro lado tá o que sobrou da mala, 90 mil mais ou menos".

Segundo o jornal "Estadão", uma parte desses valores foi entregue ao empresário Fernando Bittar, ex-sócio de Fábio Luís da Silva, o Lulinha, filho do presidente Lula. A TV Globo confirmou que essas informações foram extraídas pela PF do celular de Roberta.

Segundo as mensagens, a empresária ordenou que Ulisses Barbosa entregasse R$ 193 mil a Bittar. A Polícia Federal identificou também mensagens em que Roberta Luchsinger ordenou que o motorista dela fizesse pagamentos em dinheiro vivo a dois servidores do Ministério do Desenvolvimento Social.

articles.title: Apostas ilegais: Justiça pede bloqueio de 43 perfis no Telegram | G1
articles.standfirst: A ação é a primeira após a medida provisória de sexta-feira (25). O órgão também prepara o bloqueio de mais de 500 sites de apostas.
articles.summary: Após nova medida provisória, o Ministério da Justiça acionou o Telegram contra perfis de apostas e cassinos ilegais e prepara o bloqueio de 500 sites.
articles.body:
O Ministério da Justiça acionou neste domingo (27) o Telegram para pedir a remoção de 43 canais e perfis que divulgam apostas e jogos de cassino virtuais ilegais.

Essa é a primeira ação do tipo movida pelo ministério desde a edição pelo governo Lula, na sexta-feira (25), da medida provisória que proibiu as bets e os cassinos on line no país .

Entretanto, a determinação deste domingo não é uma consequência direta da medida provisória, que prevê prazo até a 0h de 6 de outubro para que sites e aplicativos de apostas saiam do ar.

Antes da MP, o ministério já movia ações para remoção de sites e perfis em redes sociais que hospedavam ou divulgavam bets e jogos sem autorização para funcionar no Brasil.

Esse tipo de medida, porém, deve ser tornar mais frequente a partir de agora devido à edição da MP, que tornou ilegal no país qualquer tipo de aposta on line.

Governo anuncia proibição das bets no Brasil 3 anos após ter regulamentado as empresas de apostas — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Além dos perfis no Telegram, o Ministério da Justiça prepara pedido à Anatel para bloqueio que pode atingir mais de 500 sites de aposta ilegais.

Também na sexta, o governo Lula anunciou o envio ao Congresso de um projeto de lei que criminaliza a exploração de jogos on line no Brasil.

O texto cria cinco novos crimes para reforçar a proibição das bets prevista na medida provisória. Explorar ou operar "apostas de quota fixa" passará a ser punido com prisão de 4 a 6 anos, além de multa, mesmo quando a atividade tiver autorização de autoridades estrangeiras.

articles.title: O que mostram as pesquisas estaduais da Quaest para presidente | G1
articles.standfirst: Diretor da Quaest e professor da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), Felipe Nunes analisa o momento da corrida presidencial a partir dos resultados das pesquisas estaduais.
articles.summary: Diretor da Quaest e professor da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), Felipe Nunes analisa o momento da corrida presidencial a partir dos resultados das pesquisas estaduais.
articles.body:
A eleição presidencial está empatada no agregado. Mas as pesquisas Quaest desta semana em 26 estados (e o Datafolha no PI) mostram padrões muito claros por baixo desse empate. Vou mostrar os principais.

O mapa do 1º turno tem três Brasis. Lula à frente em 10 estados (todo o Nordeste e o AP). Flávio à frente em 8 (RJ, PR, SC, MS, MT, AC, RO e RR). E 9 empatados na margem de erro, incluindo SP, MG e RS.

Pesquisa Quaest para presidente no 1º turno — Foto: Reprodução/Quaest

O voto de Lula hoje é quase uma cópia de 2022. A correlação entre a intenção de voto em cada estado e o resultado do 1º turno de 2022 é de 0,98. É a calcificação em números.

O mesmo vale do outro lado. O voto em Flávio repete o de Jair em 2022, com correlação de 0,95. Trocou o nome, o eleitorado ficou.

Onde Lula cresce? No Nordeste, onde já era forte: MA +7, BA +6, PB e SE +4. Fora da região, quase nada muda: de -3 (GO e TO) a +3 (DF), com exceção do AP (+6). Lula aprofunda o voto onde já tinha.

Flávio melhora em relação a Jair no Norte e no Centro-Oeste (RO +6, MT +5, PA +4) e até na BA (+5). Mas perde onde a direita tem alternativa: DF -8, GO -6 (estado de Caiado), PR, RS e ES -3.

Por que isso importa? Porque o jogo está nos independentes. Eles são de 24% a 36% do eleitorado nos estados e chegam ao pico no RJ (36%), no AM (35%) e em TO, RS e GO (33%).

Lula vai além do próprio campo: em quase todos os estados, tem mais voto que a soma de lulistas e esquerda não lulista, sobretudo no NE. Flávio não consolida o seu em MG, GO, DF e SP, onde fica abaixo da soma da direita.

A aprovação do governo ajuda a explicar o mapa: saldo positivo no Nordeste, no AM (+7) e no PA (+4), negativo em todo o Centro-Sul. MG (-5) e TO (-3) estão empatados, e são justamente estados em disputa.

O medo organiza o voto. No NE, quase 60% temem a volta da família Bolsonaro. No Norte e no Sul, até 64% temem mais um mandato de Lula. O medo dos dois chega a 8% em MG, SP, RJ, DF e GO: ali mora o eleitor em disputa.

Um dado curioso: mesmo onde está empatado ou atrás, Lula é visto como favorito. Em SP, 50% acham que ele vence (35% Flávio). No RJ, 49% a 37%. No PR, 44% a 40%. Flávio só é apontado como vencedor em 7 estados.

E ainda há espaço para mudança. Entre quem declara voto, de 11% a 23% dizem que a escolha pode mudar. Os mais voláteis: PR (23%), AP (21%), SP e SC (20%), MG e DF (19%).

Nos estados, a regra é outra: resolver cedo. Pelo critério mais rigoroso (líder acima da soma dos demais, fora da margem), 7 estados já têm vencedor provável no 1º turno: RR, AP, PI, PB, MS, SP e SC. Outros 14 estão na margem.

Mas aprovação estadual não vira voto automático. Em todos os estados, o candidato do governo tem menos voto que a aprovação do governo. O caso extremo é o PR: cerca de 80% aprovam, e o candidato do governador tem 20%.

E o eleitor ainda não escolheu. Na espontânea para governador, a indecisão vai de 18% no AP a 65% no MT. Em 13 estados, mais da metade ainda não cita nenhum nome.

No Senado é ainda mais aberto: em 22 estados, mais de 60% não citam nenhum candidato na espontânea. Em SP, são 79%. Se nem o eleitor sabe em quem vai votar, a pesquisa não tem como adivinhar.

Por fim, o que o eleitor cobra: violência lidera no RJ (62%), no CE (54%) e na BA (40%). Saúde é o principal problema na maioria dos outros estados, chegando a 60% no DF. No RS, enchentes ainda somam 25%.

Resumo: o empate nacional esconde um país calcificado, um eleitor independente concentrado no Centro-Sul que ainda pode se mover, e estados com pressa de resolver a eleição para governador. A última semana vai ser decisiva.

articles.title: Irmãos de bois-bumbás rivais atuam juntos pela primeira vez em 14 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Conhecidos por defenderem bois opostos em Guajará-Mirim, Jaderson e Anderson Mercado representaram o Boi Az de Ouro no Arraial Flor do Maracujá.
articles.summary: No Boi-bumbá Flor do Maracujá, os irmãos Jaderson e Anderson Mercado deixaram a rivalidade de Guajará-Mirim para defenderem juntos as cores do Boi Az de Ouro.
articles.body:
Após passarem a infância juntos na cultura do boi-bumbá, os irmãos Jaderson e Anderson Mercado voltaram a atuar lado a lado pela primeira vez na fase adulta, 14 anos após a última apresentação conjunta. Conhecidos pela rivalidade na arena de Guajará-Mirim (RO), eles defendem bois opostos: Jaderson é item do Flor do Campo, enquanto Anderson representa o Malhadinho.

Longe da arena de Guajará e de seus bois de origem, os irmãos defenderam as cores do Boi Az de Ouro na noite de sábado (26), durante a 42ª edição do Arraial Flor do Maracujá, em Porto Velho .

Na apresentação, Anderson, que já integrava o grupo da capital, atuou como Levantador de Toadas, responsável por conduzir os cantos do bumbá. Jaderson assumiu o posto de Amo do Boi, figura encarregada de entoar os versos que desafiam o boi adversário.

O g1 conversou com um dos irmãos, Janderson, sobre a experiência de dividir a arena com o irmão. Segundo ele, a parceria surgiu de forma inesperada após o cancelamento das apresentações do Flor do Maracujá, na sexta-feira, 18, na qual estava integrado um dos grupos que iriam se apresentar.

“Como não entrei na arena, na segunda-feira, 21, meu irmão me ligou era 8h da manhã, e ele não me liga por nada, cheguei a estranhar [risos]. Ele me repassou o convite da Presidente Andréia Guedes, do Az de Ouro. Passei o dia inteiro com isso na mente, e decidi aceitar o convite no dia 22", contou.

A última vez em que os dois dividiram a mesma arena foi na infância, em apresentações escolares e agremiações mirins.

"A última vez que dividimos a arena foi em 2012. Eu tinha 12 anos e ele tinha 10 anos. Estávamos juntos na marujada do Boi Malhadinho, e também tínhamos o nosso Boi Pinheirinho, da Escola Toufia Tanous Bouchabki, onde na época ele era o Tripa do Boi, e eu tocava violão. Nosso "pai"drasto era o levantador de toadas e apresentador ao mesmo tempo", disse.

Com a família historicamente ligada ao Malhadinho, Jaderson surpreendeu ao ser anunciado como integrante do boi Flor do Campo em 2024. Os irmãos se enfrentaram na arena por dois anos consecutivos, com saldo favorável a Anderson, já que o Malhadinho sagrou-se campeão em 2024 e 2025. Neste ano, o Duelo na Fronteira não aconteceu.

“A nossa disputa e rivalidade começou quando eu recebi o convite para ser Item Oficial do Boi Flor do Campo em 2024. De lá pra cá muita coisa mudou, principalmente dentro da arena, como item Amo do Boi. Deixar de lado a rivalidade e aproveitar essa oportunidade é muito reconfortante, pra falar a verdade eu nem sei o que esperar", contou.

Contudo, Jaderson decidiu se desligar recentemente do Flor do Campo, o que ele avalia como um retorno às origens:

“Recentemente deixei de fazer parte da agremiação Boi Flor do Campo, assim como também deixando o Item Amo do Boi. Hoje voltei como torcedor para minha nação materna, o Boi Malhadinho, então tecnicamente também estamos no mesmo time em Guajará Mirim, ele como Amo do Boi, e eu como suporte e torcedor.”

Para Jaderson, reviver essa experiência após 14 anos representa um retorno às raízes e celebra a união da família e dos amigos, que comemoraram o reencontro dos irmãos na arena.

articles.summary: Os interessados podem se inscrever até 4 de outubro, pelo site Trampolim SP. As aulas presenciais têm início previsto para 13 de outubro.
articles.body:
Iniciativa do Governo de SP: Programa Trampolim — Foto: Divulgação/Governo de SP

O Programa Trampolim, da Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico do Estado de São Paulo (SDE), está com inscrições abertas para 200 vagas em cursos gratuitos de qualificação profissional na região de Presidente Prudente (SP).

Os interessados podem se inscrever até 4 de outubro, pelo site Trampolim SP . As aulas presenciais têm início previsto para 13 de outubro.

As oportunidades fazem parte do programa Qualifica SP e também oferece 1.980 vagas em cursos on-line.

Há cursos nas áreas de administração, logística, segurança do trabalho, gastronomia e finanças. As oportunidades estão distribuídas entre Iepê , Narandiba , Osvaldo Cruz , Presidente Bernardes e Presidente Prudente. Confira as opções:

Assistente Administrativo com Inclusão Digital: 15 vagas, 80 horas, período noturno.

Auxiliar de Segurança do Trabalho: 15 vagas, 80 horas, período noturno.

Operador de Empilhadeira: 30 vagas, 74 horas, período noturno.

Luminárias e Luminárias Elétricas: 15 vagas, 80 horas, período noturno;

Preparo de Hambúrguer: 15 vagas, 80 horas, período noturno.

Gestão Financeira: 20 vagas, 50 horas, período noturno;

Operador de Empilhadeira: 90 vagas, 74 horas, nos períodos da tarde e da noite.

As vagas são distribuídas entre as modalidades Meu Primeiro Emprego, destinada a jovens de 16 a 24 anos, e Novo Emprego, voltada a pessoas com 25 anos ou mais que buscam qualificação, recolocação profissional ou uma nova carreira.

Além das oportunidades presenciais, o Trampolim SP oferece 1.980 vagas em cursos on-line, disponíveis para moradores de todos os municípios do Estado de São Paulo.

As aulas também estão previstas para começar em 13 de outubro. Confira alguns dos cursos com maior número de vagas:

Assistente de Recursos Humanos: 180 vagas;

Informática Básica com Inclusão Digital: 180 vagas;

Marketing Digital na Prática: 180 vagas;

Também estão disponíveis formações na área de tecnologia, como Aplicação de Banco de Dados, Arquitetura de Sistemas, Programação Mobile, Programação Web, Gestão de Projetos de TI, Segurança Cibernética e Inteligência Artificial Aplicada para Negócios.

Podem se inscrever candidatos alfabetizados, moradores do Estado de São Paulo e que tenham idade compatível com a modalidade escolhida.

Caso o número de inscritos seja superior à quantidade de vagas, terão prioridade pessoas com deficiência, jovens, desempregados e candidatos de baixa renda.

Os selecionados receberão por e-mail as informações sobre a turma. A necessidade de confirmação presencial da matrícula varia de acordo com o curso e o local de ensino.

Para as turmas on-line, as orientações serão enviadas pelo e-mail cadastrado.

As inscrições devem ser feitas pela plataforma Trampolim SP . O candidato precisa acessar o site, fazer login com a conta Gov.br e escolher o curso desejado.

articles.title: Acidente na BR-174: quatro pessoas seguem sob avaliação médica | G1
articles.standfirst: O veículo caiu em uma ribanceira de cerca de 15 metros na manhã de sábado (26), no km 146 da rodovia, sentido Manaus/Boa Vista.
articles.summary: O acidente na BR-174 em Presidente Figueiredo deixou 22 feridos após queda em ribanceira, e quatro vítimas seguem internadas em hospitais de Manaus.
articles.body:
Quatro pessoas seguem internadas após um um micro-ônibus cair em uma ribanceira na BR-174 , em Presidente Figueiredo , interior do Amazonas. Uma delas deve passar por cirurgia. O veículo caiu em uma ribanceira de cerca de 15 metros na manhã de sábado (26), no km 146 da rodovia, sentido Manaus /Boa Vista. Ao todo, 22 passageiros receberam atendimento das equipes de emergência.

O acidente aconteceu por volta das 8h deste sábado (26), no quilômetro 146 da rodovia, no sentido Manaus–Boa Vista. O micro-ônibus perdeu o controle e caiu em uma ribanceira de aproximadamente 15 metros.

Um vídeo gravado por um dos passageiros logo após o acidente mostra o desespero das pessoas que estavam no veículo. Nas imagens, passageiros aparecem feridos e assustados. Em determinado momento, uma mulher é vista carregando uma criança de colo.

Segundo o CBMAM, 22 pessoas receberam atendimento pré-hospitalar no local e, em seguida, foram encaminhadas ao Hospital Municipal Heraldo Neves, em Presidente Figueiredo.

A Secretaria de Estado de Saúde do Amazonas (SES-AM) informou em nota que 12 vítimas foram transferidas para Manaus para receber atendimento especializado. Três estavam em estado grave. Entre os feridos, há três crianças. Nenhum passageiro ficou preso às ferragens.

Ainda na nota, a SES-AM informou que das 12 vítimas levadas para Manaus, nove foram atendidas na rede pública e encaminhadas para quatro hospitais. Quatro seguem internadas, uma delas com indicação de cirurgia. Outras cinco receberam alta com orientação médica para continuar o tratamento em casa.

A SES-AM disse ainda que todos os pacientes atendidos pela rede pública receberam assistência multiprofissional, além dos exames necessários, conforme a avaliação e a necessidade de cada quadro clínico.

Micro-ônibus ficou de cabeça para baixo após cair em ribanceira na BR-174, em Presidente Figueiredo — Foto: Divulgação/CBMAM

A ocorrência mobilizou dez militares do Corpo de Bombeiros, três viaturas da corporação e equipes do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu).

O acidente aconteceu no quilômetro 146 da BR-174, trecho da rodovia que liga Manaus a Boa Vista.

Trecho da Rodovia SP-284 é interditado totalmente para obras em Rancharia (SP) — Foto: Reprodução

O trecho da Rodovia Prefeito Homero Severo Lins (SP-284), no km 520+800, terá interdições devido a obras de duplicação da via em Rancharia (SP). Em alguns períodos, a interdição será total.

O fechamento da pista ocorrerá para permitir o deslocamento seguro das vigas até o ponto de içamento. Após o posicionamento da estrutura, a sinalização será invertida para possibilitar a retomada do tráfego na faixa disponível.

Para essa etapa, também haverá inversão da sinalização e fechamento temporário da faixa de rolamento e do acostamento.

A Eixo SP orienta os motoristas a reduzirem a velocidade e a respeitarem a sinalização e as orientações das equipes que estarão trabalhando no local.

A operação foi planejada para garantir a segurança dos trabalhadores e dos usuários durante a execução do serviço. As atividades dependem das condições climáticas.

articles.title: Instituto de empresário que depôs à CPI das Bets paralisa atividades | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresário foi ouvido pela CPI das Bets em 2024 após ser apontado pela comissão como representante do Fortune Tiger, conhecido como "Jogo do Tigrinho".
articles.summary: O Instituto OIG anunciou a paralisação de suas atividades por tempo indeterminado. Segundo o instituto, a paralisação ocorreu após a perda de recursos ligados às bets.
articles.body:
Instituto OIG suspende atividades após corte de verbas das bets — Foto: Agência Senado/Reprodução

O Instituto OIG anunciou, por meio de nota divulgada no sábado (26), a paralisação de suas atividades por tempo indeterminado devido à falta de recursos financeiros. Segundo a instituição, a decisão ocorreu após a interrupção dos repasses de sua principal financiadora, afetada por uma medida provisória assinada pelo Governo Federal que proibiu as apostas de quota fixa no país, conhecidas como bets. Leia a nota na íntegra .

O Instituto OIG é presidido pelo empresário e influenciador digital Fernando Oliveira Lima, conhecido como Fernandin OIG. Em novembro de 2024, ele foi convocado a prestar depoimento à Comissão Parlamentar de Inquérito (CPI) das Bets, no Senado Federal, após ser apontado pela comissão como representante do Fortune Tiger, jogo popularmente conhecido como “Jogo do Tigrinho”. Na ocasião, ele negou .

Em comunicado publicado nas redes sociais, o instituto informou que a empresa realizava a doação mensal de mais de 40 mil cestas básicas, além de contribuir financeiramente para o atendimento de instituições assistidas pela organização.

"Sem esses recursos, e sem que tenha sido uma escolha nossa, não temos mais como continuar essa ajuda", afirmou o instituto em nota.

A entidade destacou ainda que a paralisação das atividades não é considerada irreversível neste momento.

"Temos fé de que a situação será revertida e teremos o prazer de retomar nossas atividades o quanto antes", informou a assessoria da instituição.

O Instituto OIG não detalhou por quanto tempo as atividades permanecerão suspensas nem quais projetos serão diretamente afetados pela medida.

Fundador do instituto depôs à CPI das Bets

Durante o depoimento à CPI das Bets, Fernando Oliveira Lima negou ser proprietário ou representante do Fortune Tiger, conhecido popularmente como “Jogo do Tigrinho”.

A comissão investigava a atuação de empresas do setor de apostas online e a divulgação dessas plataformas por influenciadores digitais.

Na ocasião, o empresário afirmou que sua relação com o setor de apostas estava ligada à prestação de serviços de publicidade para empresas do segmento.

Devido à MP 1.394/2026 do Presidente Lula, assinada ontem à noite, as atividades do Instituto OIG tiveram que ser paralisadas.

A MP proibiu, do dia para a noite, as atividades da principal empresa mantenedora do Instituto, cujas doações garantiam, mensalmente, a entrega de cestas básicas a mais de 40 mil famílias, a construção e a reforma de dezenas de casas, o atendimento a instituições como os abrigos de idosos e o envio de alimento a centenas de instituições de proteção animal.

Sem esses recursos, e sem que tenha sido uma escolha nossa, não temos mais como continuar essa ajuda, e é com muita tristeza que fazemos este comunicado.

O Instituto nasceu do propósito de seu fundador, de origem humilde, de compartilhar com a sociedade parte do que recebeu. Esse propósito continua vivo, e vamos trabalhar para retomar as doações assim que possível.

Temos fé que a situação será revertida e teremos o prazer de retomar nossas atividades o quanto antes. Muito obrigado. Amém!

articles.title: Trump allies could use midterms ‘counting window’ to disrupt results, experts warn
articles.summary: Fears grow that loyalists in key states could use critical period when votes are counted to amplify false claims
articles.body:
Election experts have warned Donald Trump's administration could use the crucial hours and days after November's midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce a crackdown on voting.

With less than six weeks remaining until polls close, and control of US Congress in the balance, the post-election "counting window" is seen as as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials.

While the US president's bid to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in ballots was rejected by the supreme court earlier this month, there is apprehension that Trump and his allies could use the period while votes are counted to amplify unfounded allegations in a bid to challenge results that don't go their way.

"I think because the administration has lost so many of their attempts to disrupt the normal process in court, that they are going to use the claim of foreign interference at the end of voting days to either seize equipment or to seize ballots, whether they're legally justified to do so or not," Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser for resilience and response on the national security council, told a briefing staged by the Brennan Center for Justice earlier this week.

Some states take days – even weeks, in California's case – to complete a count of votes after an election. Control of the House of Representatives and Senate may hinge on results in states with a delayed result.

"That period, that waiting time, is where doubt begins to surface," Durkovich said on Tuesday. "And when it is then amplified by foreign actors and, frankly, by domestic actors, it starts to cause distrust in the integrity of the process."

State-level elections officials are trying to prepare the public to understand the process now, to head off a manufactured controversy later, said Larry Norden, vice-president of the elections and government program at the Brennan Center. "To me, this is the biggest threat right now," he said.

"I think a lot of people may think just because they're seeing all these headlines being thrown at them that things have changed – that it's become more difficult to vote," added Norden. "In the history of American elections in some ways, there have never been more options for the way that people can vote, and they are still in place going into this election."

Early voting eliminates most of the threats voters apprehend ahead of an election, he suggested. "The earlier they vote, the more secure they can feel that their vote is going to count, and I think that's a really important message for us to be delivering to people."

The power of doubt about the validity of votes, and the risk of Trump unveiling "emergency" measures on ballots or voting machines around election day, looms large.

"Every state in the country now has live ballots out," said Ben Hovland, former chair of the Election Assistance Commission. "That really means the election is here, and it means that needs to be taken into consideration for any court rulings we're looking at."

A supreme court decision this month upheld a lower-court injunction on the Trump administration using the US Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security to vet mail-in ballot deliveries.

But groups such as the NAACP, the National Urban League and other rights organizations remain concerned about the Trump administration's insistent claim – without evidence – that the 2026 midterm elections will be illegitimate unless the federal government intervenes.

Normally, the Department of Justice and the FBI enter a "quiet period" just ahead of elections, to avoid influencing the results. That has not been the case this year.

The Department of Homeland Security continues to pursue voter-roll lists in states that would not turn them over voluntarily. The federal government has asked states to retain their 2024 election documentation for later inquiries. And DHS is pursuing an independent "unlawful voter initiative" to find non-citizen voters on state rolls, one that an anonymous whistleblower told congress last week that is using "highly questionable data" and may be unlawful.

The federal government's claims of illegally-registered voters – claiming numbers that do not bear up under scrutiny – and Trump's rhetoric alleging fraud without evidence, "back up a narrative of fraud to undermine confidence in the elections", Hovland said.

Much of the president's election rhetoric revolves around foreign interference. Experts make a distinction between foreign influence – propaganda, essentially – and foreign interference , or directly manipulating vote counts.

"It's very important for people to understand that we don't have any examples of a country trying to interfere in the electoral process, in that technical process," said Beth Sanner, a former deputy director of national intelligence who is now director for geopolitics and strategy at International Capital Strategies.

"It just didn't happen," she said. "It didn't happen in 2020."

Election security has improved across the country, partially as a reaction to false claims about Trump's 2020 defeat.

"Every state audits its results," said Geoff Hales, former chief of joint cyber defense collaborative partnerships at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA. "Election officials across the country have really taken cybersecurity seriously."

Despite the president's insistence that the country faces a foreign threat to elections, Hale said the federal government has sharply cut staff and spending on elections security at CISA, and with it the technical assistance that once flowed to state election's officers.

"The federal support that used to be there has pulled back sharply," he added. "This means that cybersecurity services have been reduced, funding for information sharing environments have been cut, the threat briefings about nation-state adversaries that used to occur dozens of times a year are occurring rarely or not at all."

articles.title: Supreme Court vote shadows Maine Sen. Susan Collins in her first bid after abortion rights decision
articles.summary: For years, Planned Parenthood’s endorsement of Susan Collins was enough to persuade Erin Evans to vote for Maine's longtime U.S. senator, believing that the...
articles.body:
GORHAM, Maine (AP) — For years, Planned Parenthood's endorsement of Susan Collins was enough to persuade Erin Evans to vote for Maine's longtime U.S. senator, believing that the moderate Republican would protect abortion access.

Evans is now "just furious with myself" for those votes. The 56-year-old from Portland described Collins' critical vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, where President Donald Trump's nominee eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion , as a betrayal.

"I was a really uninformed voter," Evans said. "I thought any woman from Maine was probably in line with me."

The Nov. 3 election will be the first time Collins is on the ballot since the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling that overturned Roe v. Wade, resulting in abortion being banned in much of the United States. This time, Evans says she is backing Democrat Troy Jackson , a former state lawmaker and logger trying to deny Collins a sixth term.

Jackson and Democrats are hoping that voters like Evans will help flip a seat in a state the party has made a priority in the quest to retake the Senate.

Both Collins and Jackson have made an effort to appeal to women, who make up the majority of Maine's population and have had a slightly higher rate of voting than men, according to a recent report by democracy advocacy groups. In campaign ads from both candidates, women are featured prominently.

Democrats' ads have focused heavily on Collins' vote in support of Kavanaugh and describe her as caving to Trump. The Democratic-aligned advocacy group Affordable Maine has spent nearly $10 million on ads stressing the senator's backing of other Trump-appointed judges who oppose abortion. An additional $32 million has been spent by Win Senate, a political action committee focused on Collins. Planned Parenthood Votes has so far spent at least $500,000 to run ads that include a female voter who regrets voting for Collins because of her Kavanaugh vote.

Yet Jackson is facing a steep challenge.

Collins has a 30-year record of winning elections even as Maine voters have spurned Republican presidential nominees, including Trump, since 1988.

And the issue trails others in terms of importance to voters. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in September found that when asked in their own words what one issue will be most important in deciding their vote for Congress in November, almost no likely Maine voters mentioned abortion.

'I do not regret' voting to confirm Kavanaugh, Collins says

Collins has long called herself a "pro-choice" Republican and a supporter of a woman's right to an abortion. She was one of the few Republicans endorsed by Planned Parenthood earlier in her political career. In 2022, she co-sponsored legislation to put federal protections for abortion into law.

The position has put her at odds with her party but was in line with Maine voters.

In 2020, the last time Collins sought reelection, the vast majority of Maine voters in the Senate race, 76%, said the Supreme Court should not overturn Roe v. Wade, according to AP VoteCast, an extensive survey of the electorate. That included most Collins voters. Some 35% of voters who supported Collins in her successful reelection bid said they wanted Roe to be overturned.

Collins' 2018 vote in support of Kavanaugh was crucial to his confirmation. At the time, Collins waited months before announcing her decision in a 45-minute floor speech. The final vote was 50-48.

Kavanaugh later joined the 6-3 conservative majority in stripping away constitutional rights to abortion.

Collins criticized the high court's decision in 2022, but she has never publicly wavered in her decision to confirm Kavanaugh. She told reporters in June that "I do not regret that vote." Collins had said before the 2018 vote that Kavanaugh, in a two-hour meeting with her, said he viewed Roe as settled law .

But her confirmation vote is what stands out in the minds of voters like Bente Lundh, 67, of Falmouth.

"She's positioned herself as this moderate voter, but she's really chopped that down with her vote for Kavanaugh," Lundh said.

For others, Collins' long-standing record as a moderate continues to draw their support even if they are disappointed with the eventual overturning of Roe.

"I think I've tried to not have my allegiance to party make me blind to what may be a better path from time to time," said Mary Ann Lynch, a Democrat supporting Collins. "Neither party, in my view, has a monopoly on the truth and how best to do things. So I think it's really important to have people who will reach across the aisle."

Lynch added that Collins may have voted to confirm Kavanaugh, but she also voted to confirm Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, who dissented in the abortion ruling. They were nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama.

Jackson makes his case to women, abortion rights supporters

Since launching his campaign in July, Jackson has announced a "Women for Troy" coalition made up of women from all 16 Maine counties and he has secured endorsements from abortion rights groups Planned Parenthood and Reproductive Freedom for All.

Jackson was serving as a top state senator when the landmark 1973 decision was upended in 2022. He says he worked to pass "some of the strongest protections for abortion access in the country."

The Democrat became a last-minute Senate nominee after Graham Platner dropped out this summer following criticism of his past relationships with women and a sexual assault allegation, which Platner denies. Jackson is now scrambling to win over voters who may be wary of his connection to Platner. The two campaigned together as Jackson initially sought the Democratic gubernatorial nomination but lost.

Jackson also has had to explain the evolution of his support on abortion rights and same-sex marriage, both of which he opposed years ago. Jackson now says he was wrong about his past beliefs and changed his mind after talking to women. Jackson's campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad said Jackson now holds a "100% rating from Maine's Planned Parenthood."

Blake Kernen, a spokesperson for Collins, described the senator as the only "reliably pro-choice" candidate in the race.

Abortion is not top of mind for Maine voters

While Jackson is reminding voters of Collins' role in the abortion rights fight, he is doing so in a state that was not highly affected by the decision compared with Republican-controlled regions where many abortion clinics have shuttered, said Mark Brewer, a political science professor at the University of Maine.

"If you were in a state where all of the abortion clinics had closed, then that might be a bigger issue," Brewer said. "That has not been the case here."

The state's Democratic-controlled Legislature in 2023 approved a law that allows abortions at any time if deemed medically necessary by a doctor, and Democratic Gov. Janet Mills has enacted legislation protecting providers of abortion and gender-affirming care from legal action brought by other states.

A CNN/SSRS survey of likely Maine voters conducted in late August and early September found that most voters are still unhappy about the decision to overturn Roe, but that anger over the loss of abortion rights could be overshadowed by broader concerns about the economy.

Kruesi reported from Providence, R.I. Associated Press polling editor Amelia Thomson DeVeaux in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open
articles.summary: President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office
articles.body:
With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy's assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today's politicians: the swearing.

"All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before," said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. "Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language.

"Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It's not OK. It's a decline in respect and honor, period."

Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language.

Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from "shithole countries" – Trump has let rip during his second.

He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally.

A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. "They don't know what they fuck they're doing," he told reporters on the White House lawn.

Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025 , when asked about Venezuela's then president, Nicolas Maduro. "He's offered everything," claimed Trump. "You know why? Because he doesn't want to fuck around with the United States." (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.)

Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump's decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. "Open the Fuckin' Strait, you crazy bastards, or you'll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH," he posted on his Truth Social platform in April.

"President Trump doesn't have a very strong sense of decorum," said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing's place in society. "The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn't care."

Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies.

In Nixon's case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase "expletive deleted".

Trump's increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush's mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a "major-league asshole".

A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced "regret" that his remark was heard.

These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through.

Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem.

"The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession," Phillips said. "The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians.

"Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing."

In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word "shit", in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics.

Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were "full of shit".

Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: "We're done with that shit."

Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity.

Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to "get the fuck out" of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January.

Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was "tired of fixing shit that Republicans break". Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November's midterm elections, she said: "Fuck that shit."

While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care.

"The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election," argued Phillips. "It wouldn't be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain."

Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking "covert prestige" in descending into coarse language.

"There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people," he said. "People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you're really like them enough that you would be a good president for them.

"It's comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: 'Would you want to have a beer with them?' It wasn't a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver."

Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of "WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves," suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that "we are in a very strident time of political disagreement".

The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses.

"I don't see any reason why there's anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that," said Bergen. "I think the language norms are just changing."

But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. "If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely."

In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics.

"We're dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries," he said. "However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that's in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands.

"Politicians' fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn't quite as high."

articles.title: How the Trump administration is trying to defend its firing of Maurene Comey
articles.summary: Star federal prosecutor is fighting her no-cause firing, as DoJ dances around Trump’s loathing of her father, James Comey
articles.body:
Two weeks after Maurene Comey secured a guilty verdict against Sean "Diddy" Combs, the Manhattan federal prosecutor received a three-paragraph letter from top justice department authorities.

"Your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately," the 16 July missive from Francey Hakes, director of the DoJ's executive office for United States attorneys, said.

The shocking firing of Comey – whose extensive list of successes included prosecutions against Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and Robert Hadden – has prompted questions about whether it was politically motivated, given that her father is former FBI director James Comey, whom Donald Trump publicly considers an enemy.

Now justice department officials' recent defense of Maurene Comey's firing – both in an 18 September court proceeding and legal filings – has lifted the veil on the apparent politicization of Trump's DoJ and as well as his seeming desire to dramatically expand presidential power.

Justice department officials have insisted that under article II of the US constitution, which establishes presidential power, Trump and his attorney general can fire line prosecutors: employees who are not political appointees. DoJ attorneys have also invoked Comey's familial "nexus" in court proceedings and the DOJ has said in court that former Trump Attorney Pam Bondi directed Comey's firing.

But critics and legal observers say that the testimony has instead shown how the justice department has become warped under Trump and bent to his will to pursue his personal vendettas against his perceived foes – and apparently their close family members.

"It's no secret that the Department of Justice is highly politicized," said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor. "A lot of career prosecutors have left voluntarily. Others have been forced out."

"They've taken a very broad view of presidential power in many different areas of the law," he said in reference to the DoJ's article II argument.

Comey sued the DoJ on 15 September 2025 over her firing, with attorneys Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron and Deepa Vanamali arguing that she was fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both", in violation of her first amendment rights.

Comey's attorneys maintain article II does not give the president or his attorney general power to fire legally protected civil servants without cause.

"It is far more plausible that she was fired for reasons that violate the first amendment than anything else. What else could it be? What would they have us believe, that her name was pulled out of a hat? It doesn't pass the laugh test," Gueron told Manhattan federal judge Jesse Furman during legal arguments on 18 September. "By admitting there was no cause to fire her, they raise the immediate question … why was she fired, and is there some reason other than a first amendment violation for her firing?"

Gueron referenced a line in an August DoJ filing that stated Comey "is thus wrong to assert that no 'nexus' exists between her familial relationship and ability to carry about her duties".

"What does that mean? What is the nexus between her family and her job?It is not her ability to do the job. They have conceded she was fired without cause. It is not some kind of performance-based failure. So what is the nexus that they are referring to?" Gueron argued. "It can only be that they believe, because she is a member of a family that is politically disfavored by this administration, she is presumed incapable of doing her work, of serving her country, and presumed to hold disfavored political opinions.

"She's basically deemed a political enemy, a thought criminal."

During the proceeding, Furman asked the DoJ lawyer Tyler Becker: "When you referenced the nexus between Ms Comey's familial relationship or family, or name, or whatever the case may be, and performance here, what did you mean by that?"

"The idea that the government could never consider the speech, or otherwise, of a family member in determining whether there is an appropriate nexus, just doesn't make any sense in the ability to carry out their duties," Becker responded.

He continued at one stage to say: "Given there may be some trust issues or something like that from the government, in terms of giving you that power due to certain familial relations."

Furman asked: "In your view, is there a nexus between her family relationship, her last name, and her ability to carry out her duties?"

"We have not asserted any sort of nexus that exists," Becker said. "We have just asserted that the attorney general can remove Ms Comey without cause. So we have not asserted that that is the reason for her termination whatsoever."

Blain, who represents Comey, pressed on this moments later, saying that DoJ lawyers "couldn't find an answer" and "struggled" when asked about this nexus.

"The government actually said that there may be trust issues due to familial relations," Blain said. If that's the nexus between her firing, then that "clearly violates" the constitution.

As for the government's assertion that assistant US attorneys can be terminated without cause, Becker said criminal prosecution falls under the president's executive powers – and that the ability to fire without cause was in keeping with good government.

"All the executive power is vested in a democratically elected president, and the accountability for serious prosecutorial decisions must not go to people who – or to bureaucrats in the government – who are not accountable to the people," he said.

The claim that accountability necessitated unchecked firing power over workaday prosecutors appears to contrast with longstanding agency hierarchy.

Speaking in general and not about Comey's case, attorney Jackie Kelly, a former Manhattan federal prosecutor who now works at Boies Schiller Flexner, said there is a "chain of command" in US attorneys' offices.

A line prosecutor has "numerous supervisors, both direct and skip level, within the office. They are directly supervised by their unit or section chief."

"Those unit or section chiefs are, in turn, supervised by the chief of their division," Kelly explained. "Those criminal and civil division heads are underneath the first assistant or the deputy US attorney, who reports to the US attorney."

Assistant US attorneys, generally speaking, do not act "unilaterally".

"There are numerous kinds of inflection points, or decision points, where supervisors are involved during the life of a case," said Kelly, who worked with Comey at the Manhattan federal prosecutor's office.

Assistant US attorneys can be fired for cause – they're not insulated in the event of bad performance. But that bad performance has to be spelled out.

"Anytime you have power, there's the risk of the abuse of that power, so I think it's really important that [assistant attorneys general] and other federal employees can be removed for cause," Kelly said. "That's kind of far afield from the idea that the executive can, on a whim, remove someone from their job without any regard for those protections.

"It's impossible to seek justice and to do the job the right way if you're looking over your shoulder in fear that you might get fired, or if you're trying to seek favor with the executive."

For Carl Tobias, the Williams chair at the University of Richmond School of Law, Furman's questions suggest that he is not swayed by the DoJ's arguments. As for what the case says about the DoJ under Trump, Tobias returned to what many believe is the main issue: Why was Maurene Comey actually fired?

"Even the government lawyers seem to admit that she was a model employee, and she had won a number of high-profile cases," Tobias said. "That then leads to the question of whether it's because of her father and those kinds of issues."

articles.title: Trump reaffirms ICE arrest policy after confusing guidance sparks alarm among agents
articles.summary: Trump told officials that anyone in the country illegally remains "on the table" for arrest and deportation after internal ICE guidance caused confusion.
articles.body:
The Trump administration denied reports that ICE had instructed agents to limit arrests to illegal immigrants with criminal records, clarifying that there has been no change in immigration enforcement policy.

Immigration enforcement remains a central pillar of President Trump's agenda, with a promise of an aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations.

ICE agents will continue to conduct enforcement operations nationwide, prioritizing the "worst first" but also arresting illegal immigrants without additional criminal histories, as part of the administration's broader immigration enforcement agenda.

The Trump administration denied reports Saturday evening that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had temporarily instructed agents to limit arrests to illegal immigrants with criminal records.

The clarification comes as immigration enforcement remains a central pillar of President Donald Trump's agenda. The administration has promised an aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations , and officials said that effort has not been scaled back.

Fox News correspondent Bill Melugin, who spoke with Trump and nine ICE and Department of Homeland Security sources, reported that verbal guidance instructing field offices to prioritize the "worst first" was distributed nationwide earlier this week.

The guidance alarmed some ICE agents, who described it as shocking and frustrating, Melugin wrote on X.

Sources later said the confusion stemmed from internal conversations about prioritizing the most serious offenders and that the directive was the result of a "miscommunication," rather than a formal change in policy.

"There is no change in immigration enforcement policy," Melugin wrote on X.

New guidance was sent to ICE field offices Saturday evening to reaffirm that the administration's enforcement policy had not changed, according to the sources.

Trump told Fox News that ICE can still arrest and deport anyone who is in the country illegally.

ICE agents will also continue arresting illegal immigrants without additional criminal histories, including "collaterals," or individuals encountered during an operation targeting someone else.

The sources said the administration's broader immigration enforcement agenda remains in place.
