articles.title: Irish PM rejects antisemitism concerns in Ireland amid dramatic vote over boycotting Israel game
articles.summary: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin rejected antisemitism claims as Ireland's soccer players held a dramatic last-minute vote on playing against Israel.
articles.body: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin rejected claims that Ireland's sharp criticism of Israel has crossed into antisemitism as tensions flared around a politically charged soccer match between the countries Sunday, with Irish players holding a last-minute vote over whether to boycott the game. Martin, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital this week in New York, outlined why Ireland has taken such a staunch position against the Israeli government's conduct of the war in Gaza, calling its military response "absolutely disproportionate" while pressing Israel to "change strategy" and calling for increased humanitarian aid to Gaza. Martin argued that Ireland's own history — particularly its experience ending decades of conflict in Northern Ireland — gives the country a role to play as a voice for peace on the international stage, a theme he returned to while discussing Ukraine and the ongoing debate over Irish reunification. "I think for the vast majority of people it does not," Martin said when asked directly whether anti-Israel sentiment in Ireland had crossed the line into antisemitism. "We have no toleration for antisemitism, none," Martin added. NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK The extraordinary player vote came after months of pressure surrounding the UEFA Nations League fixture on Sunday, with more than 160 Irish sports figures calling for a boycott and players themselves publicly questioning whether the match should go ahead. A "significant majority" of players ultimately voted on Saturday to play the game, while one player left the squad after expressing his wish not to take part. In the interview, Martin strongly condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack and defended Israel's right to exist in security. "First of all, we condemned, absolutely, the outrageous terrorist attack by Hamas in October," Martin told Fox News Digital. "We believe in a two-state solution," Martin said. "We believe that Israel, of course, has a right to exist in security and its people need to be guaranteed of security. But likewise, Palestinians should have a right to live in their homeland in a peaceful way." "There are many peaceful voices in Palestine that I've met who want peaceful coexistence with Israel." Martin said Ireland's strongly pro-Palestinian position was rooted partly in its own history. "There's a very strong pro-Palestinian position in Ireland," Martin said. "Ireland, the Irish government and the Irish people, probably because of our own history, but also because of a sense of right and justice and fairness." Thousands have taken to the streets across Ireland since the war began, while national broadcaster RTÉ refused to air this year's Eurovision Song Contest after Israel's participation was confirmed. Ireland spent centuries under British rule before most of the island gained independence a little more than a century ago, while Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom. He said Israel's military response to the Oct. 7 attack had resonated deeply in Ireland and called for increased humanitarian aid into Gaza. "We want humanitarian aid going into Gaza. There's not enough humanitarian aid going in," Martin said, pointing to the conditions facing roughly 2 million people there, including shortages of food and shelter and children without access to education. Martin said Ireland wanted Israel to reconsider its conduct of the war, asking whether it would "change strategy" and "change its approach to the whole issue." "So that's the background to the Irish position," he said. "People are angry in terms of what's going on in the Middle East and that's the manifestation of it." ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS Soccer flashpoint Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson said his players were uncomfortable with the games, declaring: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide." The Israeli Football Association accused him of "stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy," prompting Martin to call the remarks "unacceptable." The FAI previously sought Israel's suspension from international competition. Separately, Irish soccer officials later voted to fulfill the Israel fixtures after being warned a boycott could cost the association at least $6.3 million and trigger UEFA sanctions. Sunday's game will be played in Hungary, while Ireland's Oct. 4 home fixture has been moved to Serbia and will be played behind closed doors. Irish supporters will not have access to either game. An organized campaign dubbed #StopTheGame has, meanwhile, spent months pressuring Irish soccer officials and players not to fulfill the Israel fixtures, staging protests and urging the national team to refuse to play. The campaign has also spilled onto the field. During a friendly against Qatar in May, protesters threw tennis balls bearing "Stop The Game" messages onto the pitch in opposition to the Israel fixtures. Martin has resisted calls for Ireland to boycott Israel, arguing that unilateral action could be "self-defeating" and may hurt Irish soccer without having any effect on Israel. Antisemitism concerns The dispute over the games reflects a broader debate over whether Ireland's criticism of Israel has crossed a line. The American Jewish Committee raised concerns directly with Martin in Washington in March 2025 about antisemitism and what it called the "vilification of Israel in Ireland." An Anti-Defamation League official also participated in the meeting. The AJC alleged that antisemitism had become "pervasive" in Ireland. Martin pointed to Ireland's annual Holocaust commemorations and the historic contribution of Jewish communities in Dublin, Cork and elsewhere in rejecting the suggestion that antisemitism was broadly tolerated in Ireland. He also pointed to Ireland's participation in international efforts against antisemitism and said the country campaigns against it globally. "We cherish that contribution that the Jewish community has made to Ireland," Martin said. Martin's defense of Ireland's position came before he addressed world leaders at the United Nations on Thursday, where he delivered a sharply critical assessment of Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, declaring that the international community had "failed Palestine." "When the full truth of what has happened, what is still happening in Gaza, is finally known, when the evidence is gathered, when the testimonies are heard, when the true horrors are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world," he said. "Nobody will be able to say that we did not know." Martin accused violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank of acting with "near-total impunity" and said Palestinian communities faced displacement and destruction "amounting to ethnic cleansing." He reiterated his support for a two-state solution, saying the only viable outcome was for "a State of Palestine and a State of Israel" to live side by side "in peace, security and dignity." Ireland as a peacemaker During his Fox News Digital interview, Martin connected Ireland's position on the Middle East to its experience ending decades of violence in Northern Ireland, saying "we feel we can make a contribution to that conflict resolution pathway." That role has taken on added significance as Ireland holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union, giving it an elevated diplomatic role at a time of multiple international conflicts. Martin also pointed to a personal experience that shaped his thinking, recalling meeting Israeli Rami Elhanan and Palestinian Bassam Aramin in Israel, two fathers who each lost a daughter in the conflict and later worked together for peace. Their stories are told in Colum McCann's novel "Apeirogon." "That's an inspiration to me," Martin said, adding that he had met both men in Israel. He said their work reflected Ireland's own efforts to reconcile communities divided by generations of conflict. Ukraine and a united Ireland Beyond the Middle East, Martin addressed Russia's war in Ukraine, saying a ceasefire along existing battle lines could provide a starting point for negotiations while rejecting territorial gains by force. "Ukraine can't cede territory that Russia hasn't even conquered, despite four years of war," Martin said. "From our perspective, no one has the right to go into another country and take its territory." Ireland has maintained its military neutrality while providing humanitarian and non-lethal assistance to Ukraine and taking in more than 120,000 Ukrainians since Russia's invasion. Martin rejected suggestions that such support compromised Ireland's neutrality, noting that Dublin has not supplied lethal weapons. "We want the war to end," he said. Martin's focus on ending long-running conflicts also extends to Ireland's own divided island. He and his Fianna Fáil party support reunification with Northern Ireland, but he said greater trust between the two communities must come first. "I believe in unity and my party believes in unity, but we have to work on it," Martin said. "We have to build reconciliation amongst the different traditions on the island of Ireland." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum would be called if it appeared likely that a majority in Northern Ireland supported reunification — an issue that gained fresh attention when Trump said during his recent visit to the country that he would "love" to see a united Ireland. Martin also pointed to Ireland's unique relationship with the United States, crediting Washington with playing a "critical" role in the Northern Ireland peace process in the 1990s. Asked whether Washington could play a role again in a future reunification process, he replied: "To a degree maybe, potentially, yeah."

articles.title: Cook Political Report founder: House is a ‘done deal’ for Democrats, reclaiming Senate ‘very realistic’
articles.summary: Cook Political Report founder Charlie Cook on Sunday said that it has been a “done deal” conclusion that Democrats are likely to retake the House after the N...
articles.body:
Cook Political Report founder Charlie Cook on Sunday said that it has been a "done deal" conclusion that Democrats are likely to retake the House after the November midterm elections, while their chances of claiming the Senate look "very realistic."

"I would completely agree that the House has been kind of a done deal for a good while," Cook said in an interview on ABC News's "This Week" with Martha Raddatz. "But the Senate, a year ago, it wasn't realistic to think that the Senate might flip, but now it's very realistic."

"I mean, the thing is, this is normal. It's happened to every party in midterm elections where your people get disillusioned and turn out at low levels," Cook said. "The other side is energized, turning out big numbers and then those fickle independent voters in the middle start breaking against you."

He added that he expects Democrats to pick up around 20 seats in the House and four or five in the Senate. Cook said he sees this outcome in the Senate with races in Michigan, North Carolina, Alaska, Iowa, New Hampshire, Minnesota and "maybe" Kansas.

"But in Michigan, it's where the focus is on President Trump," Cook said, referring to the Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). "Boy, it's really hurting. But when you have a Democrat nominee that's somewhat polarizing, controversial, like you have in Michigan, that takes the attention away from Trump and goes on the Democrat."

Cook said the race is not likely to be a "blue wave" but a "red undertow," saying that a wave would appear more "uniform" and that "pulling down" Republicans has hit "some places more than other places."

The Hill's partner Decision Desk HQ forecasted a 72 percent probability that Democrats retake the House and a 54 percent possibility of winning back the Senate after November.

Polling experts have said that forecasts favoring Democratic victories in both chambers are reflected in Trump's tanking approval ratings, Democratic enthusiasm in the primaries and GOP candidates publicly breaking with the president over the Iran war's effect on soaring prices.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll shows the president's approval rating sunk to an all-time low — at 32 percent. Among Republicans, 72 percent said they approved of his performance, down from 82 percent the week before. GOP approval sat at 91 percent right after his second inauguration.

Republican support for the Iran war has also been on the decline , with some like Rogers calling for the conflict " to end, and end quickly ," as gas prices have soared since the conflict began on the last day of February.

articles.title: Ex-CIA officer’s novel alleges grave dysfunction in deep-cover operations
articles.summary: A new, previously suppressed book by a former CIA officer paints a satirical and slashing portrait of the agency’s deep-cover spying program as riven by syst...
articles.body:
A new, previously suppressed book by a former CIA officer paints a satirical and slashing portrait of the agency's deep-cover spying program as riven by systematic dysfunction.

The book, "The Pickle Factory," written by an ex-CIA nonofficial cover officer, under the pen name Sam R. Oyken, is billed as a work of fiction. Though often fantastical, it contains thinly veiled true-life details about the inner workings of the agency's spying operations, according to former CIA officials.

Most CIA officers work under what's known as "official cover" and generally masquerade as U.S. diplomats abroad. NOCs, who often pose as businessmen or consultants, have no overt connections to the U.S. government and therefore operate without diplomatic immunity.

Because of the potential dangers of their missions and the clandestine participation of American companies who provide cover to these officers, NOCs' operations are closely guarded inside the CIA.

"The Pickle Factory," published in late July, is the culmination of what the author characterized as a multiyear battle against agency censors, who first rejected publication of the manuscript in 2014. The Washington Post is referring to him by his pen name, as the former NOC remains undercover.

Former CIA employees are required to submit all work potentially relevant to their agency careers to the CIA's Prepublication Classification Review Board for potential redaction, to expunge it of allegedly classified information.

"They insisted for years after I submitted the manuscript of my novel that I couldn't publish a single word, a straight-up First Amendment violation," said Oyken in an interview.

Then-CIA Executive Director Meroe Park reversed the blanket ban in 2017, but the agency then "tried to redact more than half of the book, which I fought, redaction by redaction, until they folded," he said.

Park did not return a request for comment. A spokesperson for the CIA declined to comment.

The saga surrounding the book first trickled into public view in 2015, when Oyken - then using the alias Mack Charles in court documents - lodged a $25 million complaint against the CIA in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging that agency officials conspired to fire the 13-year CIA veteran because they disapproved of his romantic relationship with another deep-cover officer to whom he was engaged and who was two decades younger.

Oyken was fired from the CIA in December 2010 and accused the agency of suppressing his book as part of a broader retaliation campaign, according to the 2015 lawsuit.

His suit against the agency was dismissed on procedural grounds in March 2016. The passage of time, and changes in agency leadership, appear to have attenuated concerns surrounding the book, and the CIA gave Oyken final approval to publish "The Pickle Factory" in early 2026.

Books by former NOCs have often met fierce resistance inside the CIA.

The 2019 publication of "Life Undercover ," a memoir by former deep-cover officer Amaryllis Fox Kennedy, became embroiled in controversy when reports emerged that she did not receive final CIA approval to publish her book. Fox Kennedy - who served until recently as a senior official within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Office of Management and Budget inside the Trump administration - did not appear to face sanction by the agency.

The CIA did sue another ex-NOC, writing under the pen name Ishmael Jones, for publishing a critical 2008 nonfiction account of his own experience inside the deep-cover program. Jones's book, "The Human Factor ," had not been reviewed by agency censors. In 2012, a federal judge ordered Jones to forfeit any profit from future sales of the book.

"The Pickle Factory" dredges up what many CIA alumni consider an unhappy chapter in the history of the agency's deep-cover program .

In addition to skewering a number of former senior agency officials who oversaw the NOC cadre - whose biographies (and, at times, names) are only lightly fictionalized - the book recounts the agency's post-9/11 push to procure, and perhaps surreptitiously redirect for other purposes, billions of dollars in funding earmarked by Congress for a vastly expanded NOC program.

The post-9/11 NOC expansion was a real-life "debacle," said a former deep-cover colleague of Oyken's, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly address sensitive intelligence operations, "where results were secondary, receipts were primary, and spending was king."

Much of Oyken's work with the agency remains shrouded in secrecy. His career bridged two eras at CIA, according to the same former colleague: the bespoke, targeted deep-cover program extant at CIA before Sept. 11, 2001, and the engorged NOC program that followed it, with younger, poorly trained NOCs being rushed into the field.

One part of this initiative involved deploying groups of these new NOCs to roughly a dozen secret "platforms" abroad; by 2008, almost all these efforts had folded in failure.

Oyken joined the CIA in 1996 as a French-speaking graduate of Harvard Law School who worked for the white-shoe law firm Covington & Burling before joining the agency, according to a declassified tranche of documents reviewed by The Post.

In 1999, he was selected for a 20-year deep-cover assignment abroad, an unusually long posting for NOC officers. The documents, some of which were redacted, point to a posting somewhere in Europe.

That assignment was cut short for reasons unclear in the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. The mission ended because of a counterintelligence issue unrelated to Oyken's performance, according to another former CIA official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe clandestine operations. Oyken was subsequently assigned to be an instructor to CIA trainees, according to the documents.

He was then selected for a managerial role inside the NOC program, according to court documents as well as the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. Oyken is identified in the declassified papers as a "QRN," which former CIA colleagues say refers to "Quick Reaction NOC," an elite group of deep-cover officers who often travel on non-U.S. passports to undertake highly sensitive intelligence-gathering or eavesdropping-related missions abroad.

The court documents suggest that, after his stint as a trainer, Oyken served as QRN chief, stating that he "exercised supervisory authority over more than 80 subordinates, including other NOC Operations Officers in his Group."

Oyken's dismissal from the CIA was a contentious and bitter affair, per both sets of documents. His overseers accused him of financial improprieties, inappropriate romantic relationships with subordinates, absenteeism in his managerial duties and bullying of underlings. Agency officials also lamented his lack of recruitments, according to the declassified tranche.

His was "a chronic case of long-term behavior that has completely eroded the confidence management has in this officer," said one declassified agency memorandum reviewed by The Post.

Oyken strenuously contested the allegations. "They came at me like a pack of wild dogs," he said in an interview.

The declassified documents reveal an aggressive investigation into Oyken, including his finances. In one partially redacted 2009 email, an incoming NOC program chief decries the "loose approach" to deep-cover deployments, vowing that Oyken "will be coming home the first day I'm in the chair." He was "the kind of china I'm looking forward to breaking" upon taking over the program, writes the soon-to-be NOC boss.

Oyken characterizes the deep-cover program as hidebound and in acute need of reform. "There's a certain kind of CIA manager who prefers that NOCs be full-time accountants rather than spies out taking risks," he said. "Meanwhile they themselves squander billions of dollars and turn a blind eye while their cronies make off with stacks of gold bars."

In May 2026, David J. Rush, a senior CIA official working on ultrasecret intelligence-gathering programs, was arrested on charges of stealing public funds, including the alleged theft of $40 million worth of gold bars from the agency.

Though formally a work of fiction, "The Pickle Factory" clearly puts the real-world CIA in its crosshairs. "It's almost impossible for outsiders to grasp how mediocre the agency has become," Oyken said. "Only a novel-length treatment could do the topic justice."

articles.title: Iran live updates: IRGC will target US ships if fighting resumes, official says
articles.summary: The Indian Ocean sits beyond the southern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.

Delegations from the U.S. and Iran entered negotiations in June aimed at a war-ending deal based on a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries.

Those talks broke down as the U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint. Trump then said in August that the U.S. would launch a "crushing economic operation" to force Tehran into submission.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy on Sunday claimed to have seized a U.S. Remus 600 unmanned underwater vehicle operating in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement published by state media. The Pentagon did not immediately comment on the IRGC's claim. -ABC News' Guy Davies

Ali Mohammadi, the deputy political commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy, said on Saturday that Iranian forces would target American vessels in the Indian Ocean if heavy fighting with the U.S. resumes. "If another war breaks out, we will undoubtedly attack and hit their vessels and destroyers even in the Indian Ocean," Mohammadi said, in comments published by the semi-official Fars News Agency. The Indian Ocean sits beyond the southern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, which have been the focus of Iranian and U.S. maritime actions during the ongoing conflict. U.S. vessels have been operating in the Indian Ocean to enforce their blockade of Iranian ports and shipping. -ABC News' Somayeh Malekian

President Donald Trump said Saturday morning that he rejected Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, though he did not go into specifics as to why he found the proposal unsatisfactory. "Well, I'm rejecting their deal. They want to make a deal where we open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump said. "We're winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait."

"They want to make a deal. I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. But I'm not. That deal would not be acceptable," he added. "And what they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait. You know why? Because they're dying. You know why they're dying? Because they have no money coming in. Because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait," the president said. -ABC News' Emily Chang

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told journalists Thursday there is a "major atmosphere of mistrust" between the U.S. and Iran, but that "we are ready for a trust-building relationship." After Iran's president addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York, he provided remarks to a small group of journalists, including ABC News' Martha Raddatz.

"We struggle to understand why America attacked Iran," he said. "We don't want a nuclear weapon," adding, "President Trump says the U.S. obliterated the program, so why do they need to inspect?" But he said, "We are willing to have inspectors." Separately, Iran's foreign minister told journalists that Iran has presented a plan through mediators that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days if the U.S. agrees to certain conditions. The minister did not spell out the steps the U.S. would have to take but said they were similar to a memorandum of understanding the U.S. signed in Islamabad but has since backed away from. With gas prices in the U.S. soaring to nearly $4.50 per gallon and diesel prices at an all-time high tonight, the Iranian president told journalists, "It is impossible for the U.S. to make Iran surrender." He acknowledged the U.S. "has the power to destroy anything and everything," but insisted, "We will never surrender." The Iranian president also claimed most of the U.S. bases in the region are no longer usable. Regarding Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was severely wounded and reportedly disfigured during the first day of the war, the Iranian president said he met with the supreme leader twice and "saw no major challenges with this health." The supreme leader has not been seen in public since that initial strike.

After a week in which more Republicans have emerged to call for an end to the war in Iran, the Senate failed to adopt a House-passed war powers resolution on Thursday by a vote of 49-50. Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins, Rand Paul and Thom Tillis joined all but one Democrat, Sen. John Fetterman, in voting in favor of the resolution. Democratic Sen. Angela Alsobrooks did not vote. Democrats would've needed full attendance and five Republicans to vote with them in order for the resolution to pass. Read more here . -ABC News' Lalee Ibssa and Allison Pecorin

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech at the United Nations Thursday got off to a raucous start, as scores of diplomats walked out of the hall in protest as soon as he approached the podium. Netanyahu wasted no time delving into the conflict with Iran.

"Devastating Iran's nuclear facilities was hard. It was very hard to do. But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make as prime minister," he said. Netanyahu praised President Donald Trump claiming Israel had "no greater partner." "Israel has never been stronger. We are not afraid. But I'll tell you who is afraid: the tyrants of Tehran. That's who. And you know what they're most afraid of? They're own people," he said. -ABC News' Shannon Kingston

Thee United Arab Emirates on Thursday suspended flights by Iranian air carriers to and from the country until further notice, according to the state-run WAM news agency. In a statement carried by WAM, the General Civil Aviation Authority said that "the decision was made in light of the US ban imposed on Iranian airlines from using airports in various countries around the world." The authority said it will continue to update relevant authorities and the public on any developments until air traffic between the UAE and Iran returns to normal. -ABC News' Desiree Adib

Saudi forces intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles on Thursday, a military spokesperson said, following safety alerts issued for five regions of the country. Col. Turki Al-Malki, the spokesperson for Saudi-led coalition forces operating in support of the internationally-backed Yemeni government, said in posts to X that air defenses "thwarted an attempt to target Taif and Yanbu," two of the five regions put under safety alert. "Escalations and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly," he added.

The Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defence on Thursday issued safety alerts for five regions amid continued cross-border hostilities with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The directorate posted safety alerts to X for the regions of Yanbu, Tabuk, Taif, Mecca and Jeddah.

All warnings were lifted soon after they were announced, with the directorate saying that the "danger has passed."

Senior Iranian figures praised Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's Wednesday address to the United Nations General Assembly, in which he said Tehran "will never bow" to U.S. threats. Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of the Iranian armed forces, wrote in a post on X that Pezeshkian's speech constituted "a slap in the face" to the U.S., after President Donald Trump said he was mulling a "big decision" at to whether to make a deal with Tehran or "quickly annihilate" the country. "As long as Iran's waters, land and skies remain under threat, no aggressor nation -- nor any supporter of such aggressors -- shall enjoy security," Abdollahi said. The speaker of the Iranian parliament and Tehran's chief negotiator, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, said in a post to X that Pezeshkian "spoke not just for a government, but for a 3,000-year-old civilization. He was the powerful voice of courage, resilience and strength for the Islamic Republic of Iran."

articles.title: Texas voters have plenty to say about whether Lone Star State could turn blue
articles.summary: Texas voters at the State Fair of Texas reveal how inflation and economic frustration are shaping the Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton races this fall.
articles.body: DALLAS — Everything is bigger in Texas, including the political stakes this November. Texas voters head to the polls Nov. 3 in an election that could reshape the state's political landscape, with major battles for governor, U.S. Senate and seats in Congress and the state legislature. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott faces Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Republican Ken Paxton squares off against Democrat James Talarico for a U.S. Senate seat. At the State Fair of Texas in Dallas, voters told Fox News Digital that pocketbook pressures are shaping how they view the state's future, with some predicting the reliably red Lone Star State will stay that way while others see an opening for Democrats this fall. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE "I think we're going to struggle, but I think it will stay red," Briana of Garland, told Fox News Digital. Mike and Cynthia, a couple from Houston, were more definitive. "Red. It's going to stay red," they said. Chris took that confidence a step further. "Hell will freeze over before Texas flips blue," Chris told Fox News Digital. Patrick and Jennifer, of Dallas, shared that confidence. "Texas will always be a Republican state," Jennifer said, while acknowledging that Republican candidates will not win every race. "But we still think it will stay Republican," Patrick added. Not everyone at the fair was betting on Texas staying firmly in Republican hands. WE ASKED AMERICANS TO GRADE THE ECONOMY. THEN WE ASKED IF IT WOULD CHANGE THEIR VOTE. Mary said she believes the Dallas-Fort Worth area is moving in the opposite direction. "It's definitely leaning more blue. Texas as a whole, I'm not sure," she said. "I think if there would be an election that swings blue, it would be this one. So we'll see if it happens." Party politics aside, several voters said the economy remains top of mind. Cynthia, who moved to Texas from New York, said she is looking for policies that will grow the economy, support businesses and leave families with enough disposable income to enjoy outings like the State Fair. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS "If you don't have enough disposable income, then you can't really enjoy something like this," she said. "It's pricey." Jennifer also pointed to inflation and the prolonged strain of higher prices. "I think people were expecting some sort of inflation," Jennifer said. "But I don't think we were prepared for it to last this long." Meanwhile, Roxanne also expressed frustration with the country's current direction, saying dissatisfaction with the current administration is influencing her political outlook. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I just don't agree with the current administration, so I really want to see somebody else come in and do a better job," she said. From the midway to the ballot box, Texas voters offered competing views of where the Lone Star State is headed, but agreed the economy will be difficult to ignore as they prepare to cast their ballots Nov. 3.

articles.title: White House airs another government-funded ad, this time with Trump warning of ‘final battle’
articles.summary: The Trump administration is set to launch another overtly political campaign ad funded by taxpayer dollars, attacking the “fake news media” and “the sick pol...
articles.body:
The White House has launched another taxpayer-funded television ad before the midterms, this time featuring imagery of President Donald Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying "this is the final battle."

"We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all," Trump says in the ad , echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.

The ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox's broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game.

The Trump administration has drawn widespread attention for its airing of ads featuring the president just over a month before the November midterms. The White House has compared the ads to previous administrations running public service announcements about Medicare, Obamacare and promoting Covid-19 vaccination, saying in a statement that its new commercials "are very clearly not campaign ads."

The latest ad appears nearly identical to the majority of a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign. The video on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump's campaign logo and a number to text, while "Paid for by the US Government" is seen across the screen at the end of the White House-funded ad.

This is the third government-funded ad to be captured in recent days by the media tracker AdImpact. An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism, with text on the screen that touts his administration's accomplishments, such as "reigniting American manufacturing."

A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, "Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one."

The White House declined to elaborate on how the first ad was being funded but defended it as part of "public service announcements" to promote national pride.

"The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic," a White House spokesperson said in a statement. "We should be proud of our country."

That ad drew scrutiny from the government watchdog group Common Cause, which suggested it could violate rules against using taxpayer dollars for "propaganda."

"I don't think you have to be a legal scholar and wonder why the president has to use taxpayer funds to promote his image" this close to an election, Carol Evans, the vice president for policy at Common Cause, told CNN.

articles.title: Khanna says third Trump impeachment would be about ‘setting a standard’
articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) on Sunday said a third attempt to impeach President Trump if Democrats take control of Congress in November would be about “setting a standard” of accountability. Khanna appeared on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” when he told host Kristen Welker that impeaching Trump, who he said has become “in my view,…
articles.body:
Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) on Sunday said a third attempt to impeach President Trump if Democrats take control of Congress in November would be about “setting a standard” of accountability.

Khanna appeared on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” when he told host Kristen Welker that impeaching Trump, who he said has become “in my view, increasingly irrelevant,” would not be a mistake for Democrats. Impeachment is about upholding “constitutional values,” he emphasized.

“Impeachment says that you can’t get into an illegal war in Iran without constitutional approval,” Khanna said. “Impeachment says that you can’t just start firing federal employees in defiance of what Congress says. Impeachment says you can’t do deals with foreign governments to allegedly enrich your own family. It’s about setting a standard.”

“And the Democrats can impeach to uphold constitutional values, and at the same time, have a first-hundred-day agenda that deals with the cost of living,” he added.

Khanna said the Trump administration should accept Iran’s seven-day peace offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enact a ceasefire, as gas prices soar due to Iran’s effective closure of the strait. He said the U.S. can agree to the deal without agreeing to all of Iran’s conditions.

“In my view, the biggest thing that we need to give the Iranians is an ironclad commitment that we will not have [a] regime-change war,” the California Democrat said. “That’s what they really care about. And you’ve got Trump going to the UN and saying we’re going to blow them all up after he had said that we already blew up all their nuclear facilities, which obviously we didn’t.”

Trump on Saturday rejected the Iranian peace proposal , though Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Welker that Iranian negotiators await “for an official response through the mediators.” He said his country is “ fully prepared ” to resume fighting if Trump authorizes strikes on Iran after the midterms.

Democrats have not ruled out an attempt at impeaching Trump for a third time between his two presidencies. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has said that senior Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform will oversee Democratic action , including impeachment, to hold the president accountable should they retake the House.

Some Republicans, including Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) and Trump himself , have predicted that Democratic lawmakers will impeach Trump if they win back the House. Jordan told ABC News’s Martha Raddatz on “This Week” that a third impeachment would not be for “legitimate oversight, but to just go after your political opponents.”

“But that’s just part of it. They’re going to investigate the first family, they’re going to investigate cabinet secretaries,” Jordan said, naming FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as officials who could also face impeachment.

articles.title: John Fetterman accidentally calls himself a 'lifelong Republican' at Texas Tribune Festival
articles.summary: John Fetterman accidentally called himself a "lifelong Republican" at the Texas Tribune Festival, sparking laughs before clarifying his Democratic ties.
articles.body: Sen. John Fetterman, D-PA, triggered a wave of laughs at a speaking event on Saturday after mistakenly referring to himself as a "lifelong Republican." Fetterman made the statement while on stage at the Texas Tribune Festival, going on to quickly correct himself and assert that he has no reason to abandon the Democratic Party. The moment came when an attendee at the event asked why Fetterman doesn't run as an independent. MAVERICK DEMOCRAT SURGES WITH REPUBLICANS AS HIS OWN PARTY TURNS ON HIM, STOKING TALK OF GOP SWITCH "Because I’m a lifelong Republican," he said, realizing his mistake. "I guarantee you that will break through. That will get clipped." Fetterman gave a keynote address earlier in the event where he elaborated on his criticisms of both the Republican and Democratic parties. FETTERMAN WINS PRAISE FOR 'GUTS' AFTER GOING TOE-TO-TOE WITH JON STEWART OVER ISRAEL SUPPORT "I don’t have a reason to," Fetterman said of joining Republicans. "But for a big-tent situation, it’s easier to be included in that big tent to say America deserved 9/11 or America is worse than Al-Qaida than being very proud to stand on the side of Israel." Fetterman admitted he believed he has "no path as a Republican," but acknowledged that many Democrats are frustrated by his willingness to work with the opposing party. FETTERMAN FACES DEM REVOLT AS BOMBSHELL REPORT FUELS PUSH TO OUST HIM: 'DISGRACE' "If the Democratic Party votes me out or expels me, they’re always entitled to do that," he said. Fetterman has been welcomed with open arms by Republicans to join the party after he floated leaving his own caucus and spurred further speculation that he would jump ship after dropping a video introducing his colleague, Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention earlier this month. FETTERMAN TEASES WHERE HIS TRUE LOYALTY LIES AFTER SURPRISE APPEARANCE AT GOP CONVENTION But the progressive-turned-centrist has repeatedly affirmed his Democratic ties, even as the knives have come out to cut him loose from the Senate. Fetterman started his career in the Senate after besting Dr. Mehmet Oz in a tight race for power in 2022, where he clinched a historically thin Democratic majority in 2022 running on a progressive platform. But since then, he has become a thorn in Democrats’ side and challenged the direction of the party. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Earlier this year, Fetterman warned that if Democrats became more entrenched in anti-Israel policy positions, he would exit the party, and has taken jabs at the party’s direction during this midterm election cycle as far-left progressives, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, have emerged as standard-bearers. Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump slams Supreme Court for blocking Missouri’s GOP-favored map for third time
articles.summary: President Trump went after the Supreme Court on Sunday for blocking a Missouri congressional map favoring Republicans. “The Supreme Court of the United States will just not let Missouri have an Election Victory. They continuously, three times now, overrule Judges who came to the correct decisions,” Trump said in a Sunday morning Truth Social post.…
articles.body:
President Trump went after the Supreme Court on Sunday for blocking a Missouri congressional map favoring Republicans.

“The Supreme Court of the United States will just not let Missouri have an Election Victory. They continuously, three times now, overrule Judges who came to the correct decisions,” Trump said in a Sunday morning Truth Social post.

“Thank you to the Governor, and all of the Great People of Missouri, who are fighting so hard for Fairness and Election Security,” the president added. “Such tremendous Spirit and Love of our Country. I won Missouri BIG, all three times, and I couldn’t be more proud of doing so.”

On Friday, the Supreme Court again stopped a directive for Missouri Republicans to use their favored congressional map, and officials now have to go back to an older map for the upcoming election.

The court’s ruling was damaging for Republicans, who had pushed for a more favorable 7-1 House map in time for this year’s midterms, rather than an older 6-2 map.

Republicans passed the 7-1 congressional map last year and used it for primaries last month. However, the Supreme Court’s ruling now requires Missouri to use different congressional lines for the general election.

The legal battle over the congressional map in the Show Me State came back to the high court for a third time late Tuesday. The Supreme Court had ruled against the Republicans twice before, but those decisions were technically interim.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday had issued a final ruling backing the Republicans, saying it was unconstitutional to make officials go back to the old map because they already had the primaries with the new boundaries.

The Hill has reached out to the Supreme Court for comment.

articles.title: Manchin says ‘if character means anything, you can’t vote for Ken Paxton’
articles.summary: Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) took aim at Senate candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) on Sunday, deriding his “character.” During an interview with NewsNation’s Chris Stirewalt on “The Hill Sunday,” Manchin was asked about Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. “I don’t know that young man and things he’s said I’m discouraged…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) took aim at Senate candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) on Sunday, deriding his “character.”

During an interview with NewsNation’s Chris Stirewalt on “The Hill Sunday,” Manchin was asked about Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.

“I don’t know that young man and things he’s said I’m discouraged about, but I can tell you, if character means anything, you can’t vote for Ken Paxton, if character means anything, because he has none,” Manchin said. “So, you have a situation there.”

While Democrats usually face electoral struggles in the Lone Star State, Paxton comes with notable baggage. He previously faced impeachment in the Texas House on corruption charges before he was later acquitted in the Texas Senate three years ago.

In a recent poll, Talarico had a slight lead over Paxton. The NBC 5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group survey found that 46 percent of registered voter respondents supported Talarico, while 43 percent backed Paxton.

The national political environment has also been recently rough for the GOP, with President Trump’s approval rating recently slumping, the unpopular war in Iran nearing the seven-month mark, widespread concerns about the cost of living and Republicans falling behind Democrats on key issues like immigration and health care in recent polling.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating on Sunday evening was sitting at 38.8 percent, with his disapproval rating at 59.6 percent.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Texas Senate race as a “toss up.”

The Hill has reached out to Paxton’s campaign for comment.

articles.title: Susie Wiles reveals brutal toll of fighting cancer while running Trump’s White House
articles.summary: Susie Wiles reveals what it was like to undergo chemotherapy while leading the White House staff, saying some days just getting out of bed was a test.
articles.body: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is opening up about the grueling reality of fighting breast cancer while holding one of Washington's most demanding jobs, revealing that some days simply getting out of bed and going to work took all the strength she had. In an op-ed published Sunday in USA Today, Wiles described what it was like to undergo chemotherapy while continuing to lead the White House staff for President Donald Trump. The disease occupied her thoughts from the moment she woke up and sometimes even while she slept, she wrote. "Fighting cancer is brutal and unrelenting," Wiles wrote. Questions about treatment, test results and what might come next could overtake even a strong mind. At times, she acknowledged, they overtook hers. CANCER-RELATED BRAIN FOG MAY IMPROVE WITH 2 SIMPLE TREATMENTS, SCIENTISTS SAY Some days, Wiles said, she poured her strength into fighting the disease. On others, getting out of bed, getting dressed and going to work was its own test. "Most days, I carried the full weight of both," she wrote. Work gave her a purpose beyond appointments, scans and side effects. "Cancer can make your world very small," Wiles wrote. She said she pushed herself to stay focused on the people who depended on her, even as she knew others might question whether she could still lead effectively. KAI TRUMP REVEALS HOW FAMILY RALLIED AROUND MOM VANESSA AMID BREAST CANCER BATTLE: ‘IT’S A LONG JOURNEY’ The treatment did take a toll on her stamina, mobility and, at times, her focus. Wiles said she could not always be everywhere she wanted to be. Colleagues inside and outside the White House stepped in, while her two daughters, extended family, friends and medical team helped carry her through the illness. Wiles made clear that working through treatment would not be right or possible for everyone. For her, she wrote, the job helped her hold on to a sense of who she was beyond the disease. CANCER SURVIVORS MAY SEE SURPRISING BENEFITS FROM ONE SPECIFIC EXERCISE, STUDY SAYS After successful surgery, pathology showed no residual cancer, Wiles wrote. She said she now faces the work of rebuilding what treatment took from her. "Chemotherapy is, in a word, a b----," she wrote. DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES In a post on X Sunday, Wiles said she rarely writes about herself but wanted to share what it was like to fight cancer while continuing to do a job she loves. "Cancer tried to make my world smaller. I was determined not to let it," she wrote, adding that she hoped her account could offer strength to someone still fighting the disease. VANESSA TRUMP REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN EMOTIONAL STATEMENT: 'I AM STAYING FOCUSED AND HOPEFUL' Wiles announced Sept. 16 that she was cancer free after receiving clear pathology results following an appointment at the Mayo Clinic. She had disclosed her early-stage breast cancer diagnosis in March. Trump praised Wiles during her treatment, saying in a prerecorded May tribute that she was winning her cancer battle. Wiles thanked him for his kindness and compassion, and credited her family, friends, colleagues and doctors with helping her through the ordeal. For others going through treatment, Wiles offered a message of hope. "Cancer does not have to take away who you are," she wrote. She said that for her, life beyond the disease includes serving Trump and the country and being a mother, grandmother and friend. "A strong woman isn’t loud in her strength; she’s steady and unshakable," she wrote. "You are our champion. So incredibly proud of you, Mom."

articles.title: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day boss
articles.summary: World News Day aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.
articles.body:
More than 1,000 news providers around the world have signed up to support World News Day on Monday, which aims to promote the role of journalism at a time when organisers say the industry faces an "existential threat".

Participating media organisations, including the New York Times, Reuters and the Kyiv Independent, are sharing editorials, ads and cartoons to highlight the value of "trusted journalism".

Trust in news dropped to a new low globally in 2026, according to the Reuters Institute's latest Digital News Report , which noted that people are increasingly turning to social media and AI chatbots for news.

Branko Brkic, co-organiser of World News Day, said media organisations that were once rivals must work together, adding: "If we do not change the game, we are just not going to exist."

World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.

It comes against a backdrop of what the recent Reuters Institute report described as "anxiety, disengagement, and cynicism" towards news among the public, "but also openness to new sources and formats, and continued belief in what news at its best can offer".

Social media and video networks overtook news organisations' own websites and apps as the main source of online news last year, but are trusted less, the report said.

In another report, published earlier this month, UK media regulator Ofcom also said people now get news from a wider variety of sources, with YouTube "growing rapidly" and 20% of people using AI tools to access news.

But growing choice has gone hand-in-hand with greater uncertainty about who and what to believe, and traditional providers are still seen as more trustworthy, accurate and impartial than online platforms, Ofcom said.

Brkic, who founded South Africa's Daily Maverick, accepts that the media landscape has changed, and said established news organisations must respond.

"The old days are not coming back. We need to form a new equilibrium, and the only way we can do it is that if we actually join forces," he said.

"If we continue like this, we're just going to be weak individual players waiting to be taken out. If we don't change something pretty fundamentally and pretty urgently, we're just going to be roadkill."

Brkic said the mainstream media has "committed mistakes", but professional and reliable journalists play a vital role in society.

"We need to talk to our audiences and explain to them, it's not in your interest not to choose truth and trust," he said.

"We cannot function without a thing called the truth, without facts."

The definition of "the truth" is often contested, however, as seen in US President Donald Trump's long-running battle with what he labels the "fake news media".

Brkic added: "This is the information-based society. We are the infrastructure for that information-based society. And that society is actually going to really struggle without us."
